package_info.package_versions: 5.3.0 to 5.3.17, 5.2.0 to 5.2.19, and older unsupported versions (as per CVE-2022-22965)
package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of the spring-web package contain a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability (SpringShell/Spring4Shell, CVE-2022-22965). This vulnerability allows attackers to exploit unsafe class property binding in Spring MVC and Spring WebFlux applications running on JDK 9 or later, enabling arbitrary modification of internal server properties via crafted HTTP requests. This can result in arbitrary file writes (such as web shells) and full remote code execution on the server.

execution_context.trigger: During HTTP request processing at runtime
execution_context.file_location: Core Spring Web classes, such as org.springframework.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet and org.springframework.web.bind.WebDataBinder
required_permissions: filesystem (to write files, e.g., web shells or log files)
JVM process control (to modify internal class properties)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During HTTP request processing at runtime, the code binds HTTP request parameters to internal Java class properties using property binding, allowing attacker-supplied parameters to traverse the object graph and modify sensitive fields such as logging patterns or file paths, resulting in arbitrary file writes or remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Binding attacker-controlled HTTP parameters directly to internal server class properties is highly suspicious, as it enables modification of critical server configuration and behavior, such as log file locations and patterns, which can be leveraged to write malicious files (e.g., web shells) to the server.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, property binding in web frameworks is restricted to safe, whitelisted fields corresponding to user input (e.g., form fields). This vulnerability allows unfiltered access to deep internal properties, violating the expectation of strict separation between user input and server internals.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate property binding is used to map user input from web forms to data objects (e.g., binding 'username' or 'email' fields). It is never intended to allow modification of internal server properties such as classLoader or pipeline fields.
key_indicators: HTTP request parameters with deeply nested names targeting internal Java class properties (e.g., class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern)
Lack of property name filtering or whitelisting in property binding logic
Ability to modify server log configuration or file paths via HTTP requests
Creation of new files (e.g., JSP web shells) in web application directories as a result of crafted requests

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted HTTP request containing parameters with names targeting internal Java class properties (e.g., class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern) to the vulnerable Spring application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Modification of internal server configuration, such as log pattern or file location, by binding attacker-supplied values to sensitive fields.

attack_chain.action: The server processes the request and, due to unsafe property binding, applies the malicious parameters to internal fields, enabling the attacker to write arbitrary files (such as a JSP web shell) to the server's web root or other sensitive locations.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution or deployment of a web shell, granting the attacker full control over the server.

behavioral_signatures: HTTP requests containing parameters with deeply nested names such as class.module.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern
Unexpected changes to server log patterns or log file locations at runtime
Creation of new files (e.g., JSP web shells) in web application directories following HTTP requests with suspicious parameters
Unusual property binding activity involving internal server classes
file_indicators: Unexpected JSP or other executable files (e.g., .jsp, .war) appearing in web root directories
Modified log files or log configuration files in application directories
Newly created files with attacker-supplied names or content in web-accessible locations
network_indicators: Unusual HTTP POST or GET requests with deeply nested parameter names targeting internal Java class properties
Outbound connections from the server to external IPs or domains after exploitation (e.g., command and control callbacks or web shell traffic)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor HTTP traffic for requests containing suspicious, deeply nested parameter names that target internal Java class properties (such as classLoader, pipeline, or logging fields). Implement file integrity monitoring to detect new or modified files in web application directories, especially executable files like JSPs. Use runtime security monitoring to detect changes in log configuration or unexpected file writes by the application process. Correlate these events with HTTP requests to identify exploitation attempts.
